sections.h2: The input layer is three problems wearing one UI
paras: The three entry points look like one feature in the interface, but they are not the same problem — and treating them as the same problem is where naive pipelines break.

subsections.h3: URL to Video: extraction without hallucination
paras: A product page is an uncontrolled input. Some pages expose clean structured data; others are dynamic, partially rendered, or inconsistent between regions. The ingestion layer has to extract the product title, images, feature claims, pricing context, and CTA, and it has to do so without inventing claims the page never made. When extraction is uncertain, we preserve source references and let the user correct the brief before generation. That correction step is not a UX nicety; it is a reliability mechanism.

subsections.h3: Image to Video: fidelity is the hard constraint
paras: Starting from a single product photo looks simpler than parsing a URL, but it is harder in one specific way: the output must still look like the product being sold. Users can add up to seven reference photos to improve consistency, and the system uses them to anchor product identity across generated motion. The failure mode here is subtle — a video that looks great but drifts from the actual product is worse than a video that fails outright, because it ships.

subsections.h3: Text to Video: exposing the plan before spending credits
paras: A creative brief is the most controllable input, and we treat it that way. The system converts the brief into an editable storyboard and generates the selected shots only after the user has seen the plan. This is deliberate: it turns an open-ended generation into a reviewable decision, and it keeps credit spend tied to an approved intent.

sections.h2: The planning layer is where most of the product lives
paras: If the input layer is about fidelity, the planning layer is about judgment. The system has to answer a set of questions that a human creative director would answer: What is the hook? Who is on camera? What does the script claim? Which proof points appear, and in what order? What is the call to action? How many scenes does that require?

This is also where the presenter model choice matters. [AI Actor](/ai-actors) pairs an avatar with a script and voiceover for talking-head UGC. **AI Twin** builds a digital clone for founder-led content. [AI Presenter](/ai-video-generation/spokesperson-video) handles product explanations and demos. Each option changes the planning constraints — a talking head needs different pacing and proof than a feature demo.
sections.callout: We made a deliberate decision not to require users to learn prompt engineering. That is not a marketing line; it is an architectural one. The planning layer absorbs complexity so the interface does not expose it.

sections.h2: The generation layer has to be boring on purpose
sections.code:
job lifecycle:
  queued -> planning -> generating -> rendering -> ready
                  \         |             /
                   \________|____________/
                            |
                            v
                    failed -> credits released
paras: Once a plan is approved, the generation layer orchestrates video model calls, presenter rendering, text-to-speech, captions, transitions, and final assembly. The output target is HD, watermark-free, creator-style video suitable for product pages or social channels.

The interesting engineering here is not the model call — it is everything around it. The assembly layer is built on deterministic job IDs, idempotent steps, retries with backoff, and explicit state transitions. A user should never have to guess whether a job is queued, planning, generating, rendering, or failed.
afterCode: Boring is a feature. A pipeline that behaves the same way every time is what lets a team build a weekly testing cadence on top of it.

sections.h2: The metering layer is a promise about money
paras: Usage-based credits are usually described as a pricing model. From the engineering side, they are a consistency problem: the balance the user sees has to match the work the system actually performed, at every moment, including when things fail.

We run credits on a reserve-commit-release model. Credits are reserved when a job starts, committed when the final render succeeds, and released automatically when a job fails. A 15-second video consumes 20 credits, a 30-second video consumes 40, a product photo consumes 1. The packaging is [buy-once with credits delivered monthly](/pricing): Starter at $24/month for 200 credits, Pro at $59/month for 500, Studio at $129/month for 1,200.
sections.blockquote: The test I hold the metering layer to is simple: a failed job should never require a support ticket to get credits back. If it does, the system failed before the user noticed.

sections.h2: The boundary layer: consent, identity, and restraint
paras: AI Twin is the feature that raises the hardest questions, and it should. A digital clone that looks, speaks, and moves like a person requires explicit consent, identity verification, and controlled access. We treat customer assets as customer assets: signed URLs, access control, retention policies, and no training on customer data without permission.

There is also a quality boundary worth stating plainly. We are not trying to make every video look like a studio production. We are trying to preserve what makes creator video work — the fast hook, conversational delivery, product proof, and clear CTA. When a job fails those checks, the right outcome is a clear failure state and an automatic credit release, not a polished-looking video that misrepresents the product.

The system runs on a queue-based orchestration layer with model routing, capacity management, caching where it helps, and observability across every stage. We track success rate, latency, credit reconciliation, and failure reasons. Those metrics are not vanity numbers — they are the inputs to the decision about whether the promise holds.

The next investments are scene-level control, brand kits, team workflows, localization, and API access for agencies and platforms generating creative at scale. Each of those is really the same problem in a new form: keep the output predictable while widening what the system can accept as input.

Naruebet's version of the thesis is that AI UGC video should start with a link, not a six-month pilot. I agree, and from where I sit the thesis has a second half: starting with a link only matters if the system behind the link is dependable enough to build a testing cadence on.

That is the difference between a campaign that waits on assets and one that ships on schedule. The first is a production problem. The second is an engineering one — and it is the one we are solving at BLYDEY.

paras: You'll learn how Product Links imports a product page into your library, what to check before you generate from imported assets, and how package-locked prompts keep the box honest. The example is a real unboxing clip generated on this site — the same launch-week structure you'll build in step three.

Paste a product page URL, and the importer brings the listing into your workspace as a product card: the photos, the title, the details. From then on, every tool in the workspace can start from that card. Briefs reuse the real specs instead of your memory of them; prompts reference photos that came from the listing itself.

The import also changes where errors come from. When you type product details by hand, typos become wrong claims in finished videos. When the details come from the import, the error to guard against is different: the listing itself being out of date. That's what step two is for.

In the workspace's create menu, [Product Links](/app/create/product) is the import surface: paste a URL, confirm, and the product card lands in your [library](/app/create/library) with the listing's photos and details attached.

One import serves every later job — video ads, unboxings, product demos, even image sets. It's the reason a two-person team can run a whole launch week without writing the same product description twice.
Open Product Links, paste the URL, confirm the import. The card appears in your library in seconds. Nothing is generated yet — the import only gathers the raw material your next jobs will use.

Products you import stay in the library for reuse: the same card feeds next month's variant videos and the image set for a new marketplace. Most shops import once per product and never touch Product Links again until the listing changes — the card only needs re-importing when the page itself changes.

paras: Imported photos are supplier photos until you verify them, and supplier photos go stale. Open the product card and confirm three things. First: the photos show the package customers actually receive today — listings often carry last season's packaging. Second: the details match the live listing you're selling from, not a draft from months ago. Third: nothing ships in the box that the camera won't see — if the video shows tissue paper, the box needs tissue paper.

This check takes two minutes and prevents the classic launch failure: a video that shows a box nobody receives. If the packaging changed, re-import and regenerate — the clip must always match what ships.

sections.h2: Step 3: Generate From the Product Card
paras: Start a video from the product card; the reference photos come from the import. For unboxing and packaging shots, lock the package in the prompt — here's the real prompt behind the example below:

prompt.body:
This is a 30-second vertical TikTok Shop product-promotion video, filmed on a phone in an authentic UGC style. Use natural light and a realistic everyday setting, and keep the image clear throughout.

Shot 1 [0-3 sec] Close-up: In the living room, she holds a sealed cardboard box up to the camera. Spoken line: "It finally came. Let's open it."
Shot 2 [3-9 sec] Medium shot: She slices through the packing tape and opens the box flaps. Spoken line: "I've been waiting on this all week."

Negative prompt: no readable text, numbers, signs or labels anywhere in the frame; no logos, brand marks or watermark; no extra or swapped product…

paras: The lock is what keeps launch honest: the box in the clip is the box the shopper opens. The reveal is the beat shoppers remember — closed box, the slice open, the first item lifted out. Every part of that memory has to match the delivery they actually receive, or the ad costs you trust instead of building it.
That's also why imported assets beat typed descriptions for launch content: the import carries the photos of the package as it ships today, and step two made sure those photos are current.

sections.h2: Where Launch Week Goes From Here
paras: One import powers the whole launch. The teaser and the reveal fit in a 15-second cut — 20 credits; the closer look has room at 30 — 40 credits. Keep one [AI presenter](/ai-actors) across the set so the same face opens the teaser, lifts the lid, and demonstrates the action. Burn the launch date and the early price in [Subtitle Studio](/app/create/subtitles) — typed by you, never generated.

A home goods brand runs the teaser three days out, the reveal on launch morning, and the closer look the same evening — one import, one presenter, one afternoon of generation. A gift brand runs the reveal in two languages for two markets; the storyboard and the box stay identical, only the voice changes. When you want the prompt-level view for the ad itself, the [AI video prompt tutorial](/blog/ai-ugc-video-ads-guide) picks up where this import leaves off.

This is a 30-second vertical TikTok product-promotion video, filmed on a phone in an authentic UGC style. Use natural light and a realistic everyday setting, and keep the image clear throughout. Image 1 shows the product for this video; the product must have no legible brand text.

Shot 1 [0-3 sec] Close-up: Seated at a wooden desk, she holds the green notebook and pen up to the camera. Spoken line: "Desk tour. Everything here has a job."
Shot 2 [3-10 sec] Medium shot: She points to the wooden desk tray holding paper clips and sticky notes. Spoken line: "This tray keeps all the little stuff in one spot, so my desk stays clear."

If your product has details on several sides, you can add up to seven reference photos on video jobs. Keep Image 1 as the canonical front view — the prompt locks to that image specifically.

sections.h2: Step 2: Pick a Type, Then Optimize
paras: Every job starts from a type: general product video, product ad, TikTok ad, UGC review, social Reels, cinematic launch, or how-to demo. The type sets pacing and shot structure before a single line of your prompt is read — a UGC review reads like a customer's phone video, a cinematic launch reads like a brand film.

Then press Optimize. It rewrites your draft against the type: tightening the scene, the actions, the spoken lines and the sound design. The output uses the same six-part anatomy you'll learn below, which is exactly why learning the anatomy matters — you can edit the optimized prompt with intent instead of accepting it blind.

sections.h2: Step 3: Write the Prompt in Six Parts
paras: The workspace prompt follows a fixed anatomy. Here is the real prompt behind the frother example, reduced to its skeleton — write yours in the same order and you'll get the same discipline:

prompt.body:
This is a 30-second vertical TikTok Shop product-promotion video, filmed on a phone in an authentic UGC style. Use natural light and a realistic everyday setting, and keep the image clear throughout.

Image 1 shows the product for this video. Match its appearance, color, and packaging exactly to Image 1. There must be no text or brand marks on the product or packaging.

Character: a woman in her twenties, hair tied in a bun, wearing light-colored loungewear, no jewelry.

Shot 1 [0-3 sec] Close-up: In a bright morning kitchen, she holds up the black milk frother. Spoken line: "Here's how I make a café iced latte at home."
Shot 2 [3-9 sec] Medium shot: She pours cold milk into a glass jar. Spoken line: "Cold milk in a jar."
Shot 3 [9-18 sec] Close-up: She froths the milk in the jar; it quickly turns into thick, creamy foam. Spoken line: "A few seconds with this frother, and look at that foam."

Audio: Natural spoken English dialogue, together with pouring milk, the frother buzzing, and ice cubes clinking. No background music.

Negative prompt: background music, subtitles, on-screen text, text on the packaging, watermarks, logos, extra fingers, deformed hands, duplicate people, blurred backgrounds…
prompt.label: Real prompt

parts.text: The first line sets the frame: duration + aspect ratio + platform + style. The generator reads it for pacing and cut density.
Reference lock: Image 1 is the only product reference — same shape, color and packaging, no text or brand marks. All product consistency lives here; describing the product twice invites drift.
The person is described once — age range, hair, outfit, jewelry, language and tone. Every later Shot reuses them without re-describing.
The Shot timeline: one action per shot, with a time range and a shot size. Spoken lines are casual speech, one idea each — that is what keeps the clip sounding human.
The sound layer: dialogue plus environment effects (pouring, buzzing, ice). Say whether you want background music — anything left unsaid is left to the model.
The safety net: watermarks, captions, on-screen text, extra fingers, warped hands, depth blur. Forbidding the commonest failures up front is cheap insurance.

sections.h2: Step 5: Set Length, Size, and Credits

img.alt: You can post the closing shot: hands shut the gray skincare jar on a neutral bedroom dresser.

paras: Clips run 15 or 30 seconds — 20 or 40 credits, with the exact cost shown before the job starts and failed jobs refunded automatically. A 15-second ad runs 20 credits, so most shops test two or three openings before scaling the winner. Pick the size for where the ad will run: 9:16 for TikTok, Reels and Shorts; 1:1 for feed placements; 16:9 for YouTube and product pages.

Watch the clip on a phone at full volume before you watch it anywhere else — that's where your audience meets it. Read the subtitles line by line against the spoken audio. Compare the product against the real thing in daylight: color, visible parts, every label letter. If the voice lands but one scene is off, regenerate just that scene; if it's only the words, [Subtitle Studio](/app/create/subtitles) burns new captions onto the finished file without regenerating anything.

img.alt: You start as the jar comes out of the tote: hands pull the gray skincare jar onto the bathroom counter.

paras: Structured prompts earn their keep three ways. They're consistent: the same anatomy every time means the generator has fewer decisions to improvise, and your results become comparable across versions. They're checkable: when every beat is a named Shot with a time range, review becomes a checklist instead of a vibe. And they're reusable: swap the product photo and rewrite two spoken lines, and the same skeleton produces the ad for your next product — which is exactly how the template wall scales across 19 [industries](/industries) and 6 [platforms](/platforms).

There is also a hiring-side benefit. The presenter in your prompt comes from the same [AI actor library](/ai-actors) every job uses, so the face that reads your prompt today can be saved and reused next month — one face per campaign, in nine languages, without a casting call.

A serum brand we watch tests three hooks for one product — problem-first, demo-first, review-first — and keeps the one with the lower cost per view. A gadget shop runs the same 15-second ad in English and Spanish by changing only the Character line's language and the spoken lines. A gift brand refreshes its TikTok ad every two weeks with a new presenter so the account never looks stale; the prompt skeleton never changes, only the Character block and the scene.
None of these shops shoots anything. The speed comes from the structure: a prompt that writes in thirty minutes, generates in minutes, and reviews in five.
Writing ad copy into spoken lines: spoken lines are speech — "Here's how I make a café iced latte at home", not a slogan. Slogans sound like ads, and ads get skipped.
Describing the product twice: the second description fights the reference photo and the product drifts. Lock it once, to Image 1.
No timing on shots: without [0-3 sec] ranges the generator budgets the 30 seconds itself — and spends them on the wrong beats.
Skipping the Negative prompt: watermarks, captions and extra fingers are the commonest failures; forbid them explicitly.

checklist: One action per shot — the clip stays checkable and the hook stays fast
Lock the product to Image 1 in the first sentences, never re-describe it later
Write spoken lines as speech, not ad copy — short, casual, one idea each
Put timing on every shot so the 30 seconds are budgeted before generation
Always ship a Negative prompt: no text, no logos, no extra fingers
Compare the finished clip with the real product before you publish

paras: You'll learn how to write a one-line brief the agent can storyboard, how to edit the storyboard before any credits are spent, and the five-minute review that runs between download and publish. If you've read this article's earlier checklist version, that checklist now lives inside step three — the workflow absorbed it.

The [Text to Video agent](/ai-video-generation/text-to-video) sits one step before the generator. You describe the video in a sentence or two; the agent returns an editable storyboard — scenes in order, each with an action and a voice line. You edit that storyboard as text: reorder scenes, sharpen actions, rewrite lines. Only when you approve does the workspace spend credits generating.

The scene selector frames the storyboard before you write: AI presenter (an on-camera creator introduces the product), product demo (step-by-step how it works), or product close-up (texture and packaging detail). Picking the scene is half the brief.

img.alt: You get the start of the open. Hands lift the kraft lid and begin to show the cream mug.

paras: In the workspace's create menu, [Text to Video](/app/create/agent) is the planning surface: pick a scene, write the brief, and the storyboard comes back as editable text. It's the module to open when you know what you want to say but not yet how the video should go.

The agent plans; the [AI Video module](/app/create/tool/video-ads#step-video) executes. Teams that use both describe the difference simply: the agent decides what happens, the prompt decides how it looks.

A good brief names three things: the product, the audience moment, and the structure you want. "Teaser, reveal, and closer look for a ceramic travel mug, natural morning light" gives the agent everything it needs — product to show, shopper moment to serve, and the shape of the story. Structure words work like templates: hook-demo-close for a single ad, teaser-reveal-closer for a launch set, fit-check-fabric-style for apparel. The names are plain — the hook is the first three seconds, the demo is the showing, the close is the ask — and the same three beats travel through every short ad, including the unboxing and apparel guides on this blog.

A weaker brief reads like a spec sheet: "30-second product ad for a power bank, 9:16, show features." It technically works — the scene selector and the generator carry it — but every choice the brief leaves out is a choice the storyboard makes for you. Naming the shopper moment (a commuter topping up before a flight) and the structure (demo-then-close) is how the storyboard comes back already half-decided the way you wanted.

What a brief doesn't need: product descriptions (the reference photos already carry them), camera jargon, or shot timings — the agent budgets those. Keep the line human; you can be surgical in the storyboard.

What you approve is what generates — the surprise belongs in the video, not in the bill.

sections.h2: How the Agent Reads That Brief
paras: Read the brief in three moves. "Introduction to my skincare serum" opens the storyboard: the presenter, the bottle in hand, the hello. "Show the bottle and dropper" is the middle scene — a close-up that demonstrates, not just displays. "Use only the product details I provide" is the constraint the agent carries through every scene: no invented claims, no invented ingredients. "End with an invitation" writes the closing line. Three scenes, one per clause — the sentence was already the storyboard.

Editing it is just as direct. Want a second benefit scene? Insert a scene line and the agent writes the voice line for it. Want the ending to point at the cart instead of a learn-more page? Rewrite the closing line in the storyboard before anything generates. This is the cheapest moment to steer the video — after the plan exists, before the credits move.

sections.h2: From One Storyboard to a Campaign

Swap the product reference for the next SKU and the structure carries. A two-person shop storyboards its launch set on Monday, generates between customer emails, and schedules all three clips from the [library](/app/create/library). An agency keeps approved briefs in Teams & Brands so every client's videos use reviewed wording.
